title: Distilling Large-Scale Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials to Predict Long-Timescale Electrolyte Transport Properties

method_excerpt:
Reference data for training the distilled models is generated with UMA-OMol (checkpoint uma-s-1p1) using its OMol task head [30, 29]. For each system and concentration we run a 1 ns trajectory in the NPT ensemble at 293 K and 1 bar using the Atomic Simulation Environment (ASE) [58], with a Nosé–Hoover thermostat (coupling time 100 fs) [59, 60], a Parrinello–Rahman-type barostat [61], and a 1 fs timestep. We then sample the first 100 ps of each trajectory to make the training configurations; the last 70% of the trajectory is used as the reference for the radial distribution function comparison between student and teacher.

Unperturbed snapshots are sampled every 50 fs from the teacher trajectory. A second set of snapshots, sampled every 50 fs but offset by 20 fs from the first grid, is collected and then perturbed by adding Gaussian noise with a standard deviation of 0.1 Å to every atom. The simulation cell is not perturbed. Previous work has found that augmenting training with Gaussian-noised structures improves the robustness of MLIPs [62]. The noised points allow the model to see a wider region of configuration space, and help stabilize the distilled potential during simulations. We isolate the effect of the noised data in Sec. . Every configuration is labeled with UMA-OMol energies, forces, and the full stress tensor. We use a 90:10 train–validation split, giving 3600 training and 400 validation configurations per concentration. When two concentrations exist for a salt–solvent pair, we combine them into one dataset so that a single potential is trained across both loadings.

We use the PaiNN equivariant message passing graph neural network [52] for our student model, as implemented in the FeNNol repository in JAX [63]. The model has three message passing layers, an embedding dimension of 128, and a radial neighbor cutoff of 5.1 Å. We also add a trainable Ziegler–Biersack–Littmark (ZBL) term [64] with an inner cutoff of 1.1 Å for explicit short-range nuclear repulsion.

The four 20 ns NVT production replicas run at 298 K, each starting with different initial Maxwell–Boltzmann velocities and thermostat noise. We use the global Bussi (CSVR) velocity-rescaling thermostat [67] with a 10 ps relaxation time. Holding the volume fixed removes barostat fluctuations from the stress autocorrelations, and the slow global thermostat leaves sub-picosecond correlations unbiased [68, 5]. We use a 1 fs timestep and save frames every 1 ps and the stress tensor used to calculate the shear viscosity every 2 fs. All MD settings are reported in Table .
blind_brief:
研究问题：在 OMol25 上预训练的大规模机器学习原子间势（如 UMA）已能较好地描述电解质的溶剂化结构。但这类模型太慢，跑不到收敛离子电导率、自扩散系数和剪切黏度所需的数十纳秒时间尺度。本研究要回答：能否用知识蒸馏，把大模型（教师）的精度迁移到一个小而快、只针对单一盐–溶剂体系的学生势上，并且不补充任何从头算数据，最终得到可与实验对照的长时间输运性质？

为什么值得做：电解质的候选组合空间极大，实验逐一筛选成本很高。经典力场速度快，但常常描述错溶剂化结构和离子关联；从头算 MD 又太贵。如果蒸馏可行，就能以接近大模型的精度开展高通量输运筛选。此外，学生势还能替教师“看到”教师自身无法触及的长时间行为。

实验设计：以 UMA-OMol 作为教师，先跑一段短 NPT 轨迹，从中采样构型。其中一半构型叠加高斯噪声后重新标注能量、力和应力，用于训练 PaiNN 学生。验证分三个层面：在短时间尺度上，比较学生与教师的径向分布函数和密度；在长轨迹上，定期用教师做单点计算，抽查学生的力和应力误差；最后用多条独立的长 NVT 副本，分别通过 Einstein、Onsager 和 Green–Kubo 方法计算输运系数，并与自测实验数据及 OPLS-AA 经典力场对比。体系以钠盐的醚类和碳酸酯电解质为主，另加一个锂盐体系作为参照。此外设置消融实验，单独考察“加噪数据”这一设计的作用。

review_excerpt:
Computed student conductivities track experiment across over an order of magnitude, and possess a lower MdAPD than OPLS-AA. Results are reported for the nine concentrated ( \geq 0.5 M) systems; at 0.1 M the box contains too few charge carriers for the collective estimator to converge. Seven of the twelve systems sit within a factor of two, and the model reaches an MdAPD of 36% (Fig. 3a). OPLS-AA is notably less accurate, as it underpredicts seven of the nine conductivities, places only three within the factor-of-two band, and has an MdAPD of 67%. Its log–log correlation ( r=0.72 ) is comparable to the students’ ( 0.66 ) (Fig. 3b). The student does have a large error for 1 M NaOTf in DME, overpredicting the conductivity by a factor of five, unlike OPLS-AA. This system has the lowest ionicity of the concentrated systems, and in Sec. we use ion-pair scans to show that this error likely arises from the teacher’s finite 6 Å graph cutoff, which causes ions to pair less than they should.

Student viscosities likewise track the experimental ranking closely; their consistent upward bias is attributable to the teacher’s systematic density overshoot. Because the students inherit the teacher’s overestimate of the liquid densities ( 6 – 13\% for the students; Fig. 2b), the simulated liquids are all over-compressed compared to experiment. Most of the reduction in space comes out of the free volume in the box (the volume not occupied by the molecules) [55, 56]. In Sec. , using high-pressure viscometry data of comparable liquids from the literature, we estimate that a density overshoot of this size should inflate our predicted viscosity by roughly three- to fourfold. Consistent with this, every student viscosity lies above experiment, by 2.1\times on geometric average (Fig. 3c). These results establish that the distilled students are more accurate than the UMA-OMol teacher itself for every transport property. Student predictions are tightly correlated with experiment ( r=0.96 ) and mostly follow a linear trend, with a log–log slope of 1.18 . OPLS-AA likewise overpredicts the viscosity, but much more strongly, with an MdAPD of 204% against the students’ 93% (Fig. 3d). OPLS-AA’s overprediction is also much less uniform, growing as the viscosity itself grows (log–log fit slope 1.40 ), from under 2\times for the least viscous systems to about 8\times the experimental value for the two 1 M TEGDME systems.
